newsitem.title: USA: GM official says Japan weakened the yen.
newsitem.headline: GM official says Japan weakened the yen.

text.p: Richard Wagoner, General Motors Corp. executive vice president and president, North American operations, accused Japan of purposefully weakening the value of the yen in order to stage an export-led recovery.

"There was one disturbing fact ... that I want to comment on today and that was the intervention in currency markets by the Bank of Japan and the jawboning by Japan's Ministry of Finance, which succeeded in once again in depreciating the value of the yen," he said.

Speaking to reporters in conjunction with the opening of the Washington Auto Show, he said the Japanese currency has depreciated more than 40 percent from its peak of 80 yen to the dollar in April 1995.

"I think the motives Japan has for weakening the yen are perfectly understandable," he said, adding "after five years of slow growth the Ministry of Finance in Japan is basically reverting to its old tricks --- seeking a competitive devaluation to promote exports."
He said the country should rely on structural reform to produce an economic resurgence rather than relying on an export-led recovery.
He said the weaker yen is being translated into a competitive advantage for the Japanese automakers, noting that their share of the auto market is on the upswing again.
"The Japanese share of the U.S. market had fallen steadily from 1991 to 1995 and now has begun to reverse that course," he said.
He said it was arguable about what the true value of the yen should be but it was certainly undervalued at current levels.
"The problem is that it is an unreal situation, we can argue about it, maybe 80, maybe 85, maybe 90. It certainly is not 114," he said.
